title: Oldest male orca on record may have been identified thanks to historical atomic bomb testing
summary: Researchers might have identified the oldest male orca ever recorded after testing for radioactive traces of atomic bombs in the teeth of whales stranded in Scotland.
content: Nuclear fallout has potentially revealed the oldest male orca ever recorded, scientists have found. The radioactive residue, a result of bomb testing in previous decades, was preserved in the teeth of orcas ( Orcinus orca ) and sperm whales ( Physeter macrocephalus ) that washed up over the years in Scotland, according to a recent study. "It gives us what we call a kind of bomb pulse," study first author Kieran Tierney , a research scientist at the Scottish Universities Environmental Research Centre, told Live Science. Male orcas are thought to have a maximum lifespan of around 50 to 60 years. However, in the recent study, published Oct. 1 in the journal Frontiers in Marine Science , the radiocarbon signature identified in one stranded male suggested he had lived to more than 65 years old. The research team noted that the radiocarbon data doesn't provide a precise age. However, that doesn't mean the estimate is implausible. Maximum ages are notoriously difficult to measure in nature — researchers can't track every animal to see which individual lives longest in all species — and there isn't an extensive worldwide record of orca longevity. "The age estimates we have from life history studies are only a few decades old and researchers have only looked at limited numbers of individuals from a few orca populations," said Erich Hoyt , co-chair of the IUCN Important Marine Mammal Area Specialist Group and author of " Orca: The Whale Called Killer " (Firefly Books, 2019). "It would not surprise me if male killer whales were sometimes living to age 65 and beyond," Hoyt, who was not involved in the study, told Live Science in an email. Orcas and sperm whales have banded growth layers in their teeth, which researchers believe form every year, like the rings in a tree trunk. To test this idea and learn more about the animals washing up in Scotland, the authors of the new study examined teeth from three orcas stranded between 1995 and 2016, and from two sperm whales stranded in the 1990s. Researchers studied the tooth of an iconic male sperm whale named Moby, which stranded in 1997. (Image credit: Kieran M. Tierney) Atomic weapons testing, particularly during the middle of the 20th century, unleashed vast quantities of radioactive material, including radiocarbon, which subsequently entered the marine environment and is preserved in the teeth of cetaceans like sperm whales and orcas. Radiocarbon exists naturally in the atmosphere, but the detonation of these bombs significantly spiked environmental levels of this radioactive isotope, so by measuring levels of this compound, researchers could identify whether animals lived through the testing era. Banded layers in the sperm whale teeth matched the atomic data, with the two whales estimated to have died in their 20s and 40s, respectively, suggesting that the layers formed annually at least in early- to mid-life. However, while the tooth layers and atomic age matched for one of the orcas — estimating the animal was in its early 20s — the other male's data didn't match at all, according to the study. The oddball orca, named KW2, stranded in Uist, an island in western Scotland in 2015. The tooth analysis suggested that KW2 lived into his 50s, but the radiocarbon analysis suggested he was at least 65 when he died. Tierney speculated that either a cluster of layers appeared in the tooth as a single year, or new layers stopped forming in later years. "We think that the tooth effectively ran out of space to put down any more layers," Tierney said. The last of their kind The banded layers and atomic data also didn't match for the study's only female orca, named Lulu. In Lulu's case, she didn't have a clear bomb pulse signal, making comparisons difficult. The tooth layers suggested she was in her 30s when she died, while her radiocarbon signal was indicative of historic nuclear plant discharges in the Irish Sea in the latter half of the 20th century, which were carried to the Scottish west coast. By looking at stable isotopes of carbon and nitrogen in the tooth samples, the researchers identified traces of what the animals might have eaten. Lulu appears to have had a higher proportion of marine mammals in her diet than the males, which seemed to eat more fish, according to the study. Orcas' diets vary across different populations, and Lulu's is likely tied to her community. She was part of Scotland's West Coast Community — a genetically distinct orca population on the brink of extinction — before she stranded in 2016. The West Coast Community is known to prey on other marine mammals . Lulu was famous for being the last known female in the West Coast Community. The population hasn't produced any calves in the decades researchers have studied it. Now down to just two surviving males, the remaining bulls are expected to be the last of their kind. RELATED STORIES This psychologist has a new theory for why orcas keep attacking boats 'It was unlike anything I'd witnessed before': Orcas seen headbutting a sunfish so hard that it exploded 'More questions than answers': Experts baffled by Alaskan mammal-eating orcas spotted near Seattle While the West Coast Community's living bulls weren't part of the new study, they are thought to be more than 50 years old. This longevity, combined with the estimated age of KW2, raises tantalizing questions for future orca research. Tierney noted that until now, orca studies have mostly focused on populations off the Pacific coast of North America. There, males have a mama's boy reputation ; they're typically observed spending their entire lives with their mothers, with life expectancy dropping significantly after their mothers die. But if male orcas are living longer lives off Scotland, and the West Coast Community's bulls are getting by without their mothers' support, then it's possible they could be more independent than their North American Pacific counterparts. "It looks like the killer whales around our shores maybe do something a little bit different," Tierney said. Orca quiz : Will you sink or swim?

title: 'I would love to discover Attila's grave': Live Science readers weigh in on which archaeological discoveries they would want to find
summary: Live Science asked its readers what type of archaeological find they'd want to discover.
content: From people's backyards to famous excavation sites , archaeological discoveries found the world over give clues about the cultures and lives of ancient peoples. For instance, the discovery of 1,200-year-old pennies in Denmark revealed that the Vikings melted down silver from the Muslim world , while an excavation of a 2,800-year-old tomb with sacrificed horses in Siberia revealed ties to the nomadic Scythians . Other archaeological discoveries are important due to their historical significance or extraordinary preservation. For example, the 40,000-year-old "Lion Man" statuette was carved by humans in what is now Germany during the last ice age, and it may be the earliest known evidence of religious belief in the world. Meanwhile, ancient texts can provide clues about mysterious and long-lost languages, such as the Linear A writing system from the ancient Minoans of Crete. Other texts, like the Rosetta stone , helped crack the code of Egyptian hieroglyphics, allowing researchers to better understand this ancient culture. Each type of archaeological discovery unearths something new about the ancient world. This week, Live Science polled its readers on which of these types of findings they'd most like to uncover. Over 290 readers weighed in, with 69% choosing that they'd like to discover an ancient text "that helps decipher a language." The comments also reflected this trend, with one reader writing: "The interpretation of a newly deciphered language can lead to the discovery of other things like tombs and documents, as was the case with the Rosetta stone. Once Egyptologists could read hieroglyphs , they could discover other information which helped them in their research and digs." Related stories 2,900-year-old sanctuary discovered on Greek mountaintop may have been a destination for Artemis worship 2 giant Ramesses II statues, one wearing a double crown, discovered by man in Egypt 'Unlike anything seen before': Archaeologists unearth a unique, 11,000-year-old statue of a person riding a leopard from one of the world's earliest settlements Other readers highlighted the importance of finding ancient weapons, which 4% of participants voted for. As one commenter wrote: "War has always been responsible for where people gather and settle down together. Weapons therefore can reveal the ebb and flow of people across the countries, which for many years never existed. This therefore reveals a lot about the specific development in many different areas and ultimately perhaps as to why we actually live where we do." In a similar vein, one commenter wished that they could " discover Attila's grave site , since no one has found [it] as of today." Another reader reflected on the importance of finding ancient burial sites, writing: "I think that tombs are the most valuable finds in archaeology." Do you agree or disagree with these readers? What would you most like to find? Let us know in the comments!

title: 'Alpha-gal follows none of the rules': Why a red-meat allergy triggered by tick bites is perplexing scientists
summary: When alpha-gal syndrome first emerged, it was a baffling medical mystery. Today, diagnoses are rising, yet much about this potentially life-threatening condition remains unexplained.
content: Sandra Tiguila, an adventurous eater, enjoyed a bison sausage breakfast sandwich while dining out in August of 2025. On the drive home, she noticed a rash appearing on her wrist. The burning sensation spread to her arms and legs, making it nearly impossible to sleep. In the days to come, she tried creams, pills, injections; nothing helped. Ten days later, Tiguila ate out again, ordering a steak. When her face swelled up, her boyfriend drove her to the emergency room. A doctor tested her for diseases carried by ticks. Tiguila, who lives in Carbondale, Illinois, had been bitten twice that June. Tiguila went home and the next morning, as she was drinking coffee with her usual supplement of bovine collagen for joint, hair and nail health, the test results came in. She had developed a red meat allergy that’s activated by tick bites. "I immediately dumped that coffee down the sink," says Tiguila. She started avoiding all mammal products — the main way to manage this rising and occasionally life-threatening allergy. Known as alpha-gal syndrome, the condition arises when the immune system reacts to a certain sugar molecule, called alpha-gal, that’s found in red meat. Symptoms range from a mild rash or stomach upset to anaphylactic shock; in 2025, alpha-gal syndrome was blamed for the death of an otherwise healthy 47-year-old man. The syndrome has only recently been characterized and is still not fully understood. Though Tiguila, who is a nurse, was aware of the allergy, she says she still failed to connect her rash to her meaty meals and earlier tick bites. As ticks have spread northward, so too have alpha-gal diagnoses. Up to 450,000 people in the United States may have been affected since 2010, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates. "It's emerging as one of the top adult-onset food allergies," says Onyinye Iweala, an allergist and immunologist at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill. Sandra Tiguila, who acquired alpha-gal syndrome after being bitten by ticks, frequently walks her dogs in this wooded area near her home in Carbondale, Illinois. (Image credit: COURTESY OF SANDRA TIGUILA) Odd, even for an allergy Allergies are often mysterious, but this one is extra weird. "Alpha-gal follows none of the rules that I was taught in training about how a food allergy behaves," says Maya Jerath, an allergist and immunologist at Washington University in St. Louis and one of Tiguila's physicians. For example, unlike with other food allergies, where reactions are immediate, alpha-gal symptoms often show up hours after eating meat. And, strangely, the allergy often arises after a tick bite. In the early 2000s, Jerath recalls, Australian allergist and clinician Sheryl van Nunen first shared tales on the scientific-conference circuit of patients with a delayed allergic reaction to red meat after tick bites. "Nobody believed her," Jerath says. The eventual unraveling of the mystery would happen on the other side of the world, where immunologist Thomas Platts-Mills, unaware of van Nunen's findings, was pursuing two parallel projects in his lab at the University of Virginia in Charlottesville. In one, his group was collecting blood samples from people claiming weird meat sensitivities. In the other, they were investigating patients' strange reactions to the cancer drug cetuximab. It would take both projects to crack the case, recalls Scott Commins, an allergist who was then part of the lab and now works at the University of North Carolina. First, the cancer strand. Cetuximab is a drug designed to stick to cancer cells and block their overzealous growth. It was first approved to treat colorectal cancer in 2004, but as its testing and use spread, an odd pattern appeared. In the Southeastern United States, more than one in five patients had allergic reactions to the drug — hives, difficulty breathing and even anaphylaxis. It took about a year and a half, Commins recalls, but Platts-Mills' group found the culprit. People who reacted badly to cetuximab, they discovered, had blood loaded with proteins called IgE antibodies. When activated inappropriately, IgE causes allergies. The cancer patients with the allergic reactions to cetuximab had IgE antibodies that were reacting specifically to the sugar alpha-gal , the researchers reported in 2008. Now, humans (and many other primates) don't make alpha-gal . But most mammals do. It's one of several sugars that cells attach to proteins to regulate their final structure and function. And cetuximab, like many drugs, is manufactured in lab-grown mouse cells. These cells had attached alpha-gal molecules to the cetuximab. That's what triggered the allergic reactions in the cancer patients. But it only happened in some of the people taking the drug. Why them? And why only in the Southeastern United States? The next clues came from the lab's other work, on meat sensitivities. This puzzle, of course, also involved exposure to tissues from non-primate mammals — so the researchers hypothesized that this allergy had the same cause as the drug reactions. Sure enough, they found that people with meat sensitivity also had elevated IgE antibodies to alpha-gal, causing a " novel and severe food allergy ," the team reported in 2009. The allergy is bizarre for several reasons. There's the delay that van Nunen had noticed. And food allergies are typically triggered by protein: egg protein, nut protein, etc. While some carbohydrates have been linked to mild allergies, a sugar causing such severe reactions was unheard of, says Jeffrey Wilson, an allergist and immunologist at UVA Health in Charlottesville, Virginia. Plus, food allergies were supposed to be all-or-nothing: A person allergic to peanuts will always react to peanuts. Not so with alpha-gal. For example, some people react to meat alone; others might be bothered by dairy or other mammal products, such as gelatin in cosmetics or medications. It took several strands of evidence to determine that tick bites can trigger an allergic reaction to the alpha-gal sugar. (Image credit: Adapted from S.P. Commins et al./Journal of Allergy and Clinical Immunology 2011/Knowable Magazine) Because those products are common, people are exposed to alpha-gal all the time. The sugar can even be made by natural gut bacteria. In other words, most people have no problem with alpha-gal. Platts-Mills, Commins and colleagues were still missing an explanation for why only some people developed this odd sensitivity. So Commins led a study of people with and without meat allergy to see what the allergic ones had in common. Might they have been exposed to some kind of fungus, or maybe a worm? No, and no. Then, a key clue emerged from a colleague down the hall. He'd had the meat allergy and joined the study, but had been doing well, so he dared to eat a sausage. Big mistake: He had a bad reaction. Testing showed his alpha-gal IgE had risen to "freakishly high levels," Commins recalls. The colleague also had itchy spots — from recent tick bites. That got the team thinking. Commins went back to his meat-sensitive subjects to ask if they'd had tick bites. Most of the nearly 200 people answered yes. The team then learned of van Nunen's work , published in 2009, bolstering confidence that they were on the right track. Everything pointed to a tick link: The regions where people had alpha-gal antibodies overlapped with the range of the lone star tick; people who got bitten developed more alpha-gal antibodies, and people with those antibodies often also had antibodies to other lone star tick proteins, the team reported in 2011 . Later, biologist Shahid Karim of the University of Southern Mississippi in Hattiesburg and colleagues found alpha-gal in lone star tick salivary glands . The final clincher implicating ticks came in 2023: Commins and collaborators at the CDC reported that people with alpha-gal syndrome were more than 11 times more likely to recall finding a tick on their body than those who didn't have the allergy. Around the world, about a dozen tick species are now associated with alpha-gal allergy. In the United States, the lone star tick is the major player, and it's spreading northward , helped by warmer temperatures and exploding populations of deer that the tick feeds on. Mysteries remain Given the expanding health concerns, the CDC has pledged $10 million to support alpha-gal surveillance and awareness among health providers and the public. Scientists, meanwhile, have lingering questions about how the mysterious allergy works. The pathway from tick bite to meat allergy remains murky. Commins, who hosts a podcast about alpha-gal syndrome, speculates that the body can treat alpha-gal as either something to tolerate or something to react to. The route of exposure seems to be key: Alpha-gal in the gut, from food or bacteria, seems to promote tolerance. But exposure via the skin is a great way to trigger an allergic reaction. That reaction can overshadow the tolerance, often temporarily, Commins says. This hypothesis fits some of the allergy's features: A strong reaction to the initial bite, or getting lots of bites, boosts risk. Fresh tick bites can also exacerbate or reactivate the sensitivity. Tick bites can prime the body's immune system to perceive the alpha-gal sugar as a threat. (Image credit: Adapted from Healthy.gov/Knowable Magazine) Researchers don't really know why certain ticks cause the allergy and others don’t. One possibility: Perhaps the lone star tick's taste for human blood, combined with, as Commins notes, its wickedly long skin-piercing mouthparts, underlie this species' proclivity to incite allergy. Also puzzling: Some people get tick bites and don't develop the allergy, and some alpha-gal patients don't report any history of tick bites. Some people have high levels of IgE antibodies to alpha-gal but can enjoy cheeseburgers freely. Others are sensitive to meats but have low concentrations of the allergic IgE. Karim, for his part, is trying to figure out what causes some tick victims' immune reactions to flip from alpha-gal tolerance to allergy. Some research suggests that blood type is a risk factor. Type B blood proteins contain a structure similar to the alpha-gal sugar, and this could promote tolerance, making people with type B or AB blood less likely to develop IgE antibodies to alpha-gal . Another unresolved question is the odd symptom delay. Wilson speculates that it could be explained if the alpha-gal sugar is hooked to meat fats, rather than meat proteins. Fats take longer for the body to digest and transmit into the bloodstream, so only then would the alpha-gal sugar gain the notice of immune cells. For some people, their elevated IgE levels will drop and the allergy will go away. In others, it lingers. And sometimes it seems to morph into a generalized disorder where people have allergy-like symptoms even when they avoid meat, says Iweala. For now, there are no specific therapies for alpha-gal. Allergists can suggest antihistamines and offer EpiPens to thwart a reaction. Some prescribe Xolair (omalizumab), a general allergy treatment that can minimize symptoms if a person encounters alpha-gal. To avoid activating or exacerbating alpha-gal syndrome, the best approach is to avoid tick-ridden areas or use insect repellents like picaridin on skin and permethrin on clothing. And Commins hopes to create a better treatment. It's known that an immune signaling molecule called IL-4 is key to the allergic response. He's in discussions with pharmaceutical companies to test a treatment that would interrupt this IL-4 messaging. Better therapeutics would certainly be welcome. Alpha-gal syndrome can cause anxiety, since mammal-derived products are ubiquitous and hard to avoid. Tiguila, when she was first diagnosed, went into a label-checking frenzy; she almost threw a bag of prunes across the room because it contained a possibly mammal-derived additive. A number of factors can influence whether a person will develop an allergy to the alpha-gal sugar. (Image credit: Adapted from S.R. Sharma & S. Karim/Frontiers in Cellular and Infection Microbiology 2021/Knowable Magazine) Related stories Tick-borne illnesses are on the rise. Here’s how to protect yourself. Multiple species of ticks in the US can transmit red meat allergy, CDC reports reveal 'Your fear is well-founded': How human activities have raised the risk of tick-borne diseases like Lyme After visiting the Washington University clinic and being advised to relax around foods that didn't bother her, Tiguila calmed down. She still enjoys the great outdoors but is careful to slather on insect repellent first. She recently received more good news: In August of 2026, her blood tested negative for IgE antibodies against alpha-gal, suggesting that her allergy might be gone. Her physicians prescribed a reintroduction protocol they had developed for patients who hit this milestone. She started with an ounce of filet mignon, a low-fat cut, and amped up the exposure from there. "I've successfully returned many people to eating meat again," Jerath says. In one study, her protocol worked for all 19 participants . Add Tiguila to that total: As of late September, she is back to her usual diet. "I'm very grateful to be cleared and not have to be so cautious," she says. This article originally appeared in Knowable Magazine , a nonprofit publication dedicated to making scientific knowledge accessible to all. Sign up for Knowable Magazine's newsletter .

title: Stars in your eyes? These are the best Black Friday telescope, smart telescope, binoculars and star projector deals we've found to raise your skywatching game
summary: We've found the stargazing deals worth your money this Black Friday at Amazon, including some of our favorite models that we've personally tried and tested.
content: Black Friday is here once again, and if you've been waiting for the prices to drop before buying your next telescope , smart telescope , binoculars or star projector — this could be the time to pull the trigger. But as we all know by now, retailers use these sales as a sneaky way to inflate their prices before the sale starts, so in many instances, their "sale" price is actually the same as it was before they put the price up. So how can you be sure that the price you're seeing is truly a deal? Well, we keep track of prices throughout the year, and use tools to check when they fluctuate. We know whether something is a genuine deal, and, crucially, whether the product is actually worth buying in the first place. We've searched the web for the best genuine deals on the telescopes, smart telescopes, binoculars and star projectors that we have actually tested ourselves, so you can be confident you're actually saving money and not getting played by capitalism. Telescopes Telescopes give you breathtaking views of the moon and planets. (Image credit: Kimberley Lane) Celestron AstroMaster 114EQ: was $329.95 now $280.45 A great beginner telescope that the whole family can enjoy. This 4.5-inch Newtonian reflector comes with a 20mm eyepiece for scanning across the sky and a 10mm eyepiece for detailed views of the moon or spotting Saturn's rings. The EQ mount requires a bit of tinkering, but it's a useful skill to have once you've figured it out, as it makes tracking objects across the sky easier than an Alt-Az mount. This model usually retails for $319.99, so a $40 saving on a telescope of this quality is pretty good. We've reviewed a smaller telescope in the AstroMaster range, the Celestron AstroMaster LT 70AZ , and our optics writer owns the Celestron AstroMaster 130EQ, which has a slightly larger aperture. View Deal The Celestron StarSense Explorer range is great for anyone who wants to start stargazing but doesn't yet have any knowledge of the night sky, and this model in particular is a good option if you want to invest in something you can grow with. The setup is a straightforward Alt-Azimuth mount, and you can use the smartphone dock to navigate your way around the sky with the guidance of the StarSense app. It has a 5.1-inch (130mm) aperture and comes with 25mm and 10mm eyepieces, giving you beautiful views of the moon, Saturn's rings, Jupiter's cloud bands and wide views of some deep-sky objects like the Andromeda Galaxy and the Orion Nebula. The price tends to fluctuate throughout the year, although on average it sits between $420 and $450. However, it's been the full $499.95 since September, so this price is definitely worth taking advantage of. Read our full Celestron StarSense Explorer DX 130AZ review View Deal Celestron StarSense Explorer DX 5-inch: was $649.95 now $552.46 Although it's very close in aperture to the StarSense DX 130AZ we listed above, the differences in optical design and focal length offer a different observing experience. This model is the better choice if you want higher-magnification observations of the Moon and planets, thanks to its 1,250mm focal length. It also has a much shorter optical tube, so it's more compact and easier to transport. The Schmidt-Cassegrain design is more complex to manufacture than a Newtonian reflector, hence the difference in price between the two. It was $579.99 throughout most of the year, rising to $589.99 in August, which it has been ever since. View Deal Smart telescopes Smart telescopes will locate, track and stack images for you, making astrophotography easier than ever. (Image credit: Future) Granted, it's not the biggest saving ever, and it isn't listed specifically as a Black Friday deal, but you can save $35 on the ZWO Seestar S30 Pro at Amazon. This is the cheapest we've seen it since its release, and it typically stays at the $699 RRP. It's an incredible way to get into astrophotography, even for complete beginners. It's an all-in-one system that automatically locates, tracks and stacks images of stunning deep-space objects for you. It's compact and portable, with a quick and easy setup and produces beautiful 4K images. Read our full ZWO Seestar S30 Pro review View Deal The smallest and most affordable smart telescope on the market is now even more affordable (but still the same size). It only produces 2K images, which is still plenty for sharing with friends and family or on social media. In practice, it just means you'll be more limited when it comes to cropping. It's been $419 since August, and this Black Friday deal is the cheapest we've seen it since its release. Read our full Dwarflab Dwarf Mini review View Deal If you're a more advanced user and have been waiting to upgrade, this is one of the best chances you'll get. You can now save a whopping $1,000 on the Unistellar eVscope 2 right now. It has an aperture of 114mm and a 450mm focal length, making it ideal for deep-sky imaging of even faint and small objects. And the electronic Nikon-produced eyepiece adds an immersive element to the experience, rather than viewing everything on your screen. Read our full Unistellar eVscope 2 review View Deal Unistellar Odyssey Pro: was $4599 now $3490 Another fantastic saving from Unistellar, and the Odyssey Pro doesn't have as much reach as the eVscope 2, meaning it works better on wider objects. The Odyssey Pro has an 85mm aperture with a 320mm focal length, which is still plenty to get stunning views of galaxies and nebulas. It also has a Nikon eyepiece that shows you how your image is doing as it's stacking — which is beneficial if you're not connected to the app. View Deal Vaonis Vespera 3: was $2490 now $1990 Vaonis describes the Vespera 3 as the "most affordable premium smart telescope on the market," and judging from its specs, we'd be inclined to agree. It has a new apochromatic quadruplet design that eliminates chromatic aberration and field curvature across the entire frame, excellent clarity even under city skies, a massive 11 hours of battery life and built-in multi-night capture. It has a 50mm aperture and 245mm focal length, with a native image resolution of 8.3MP, or up to 24MP with covalENS mosaic mode. View Deal Vaonis Vespera Pro 2: was $2990 now $2490 If you liked the sound of the Vespera 3 but wanted something a little more powerful, the Vespera Pro 2 is $500 off for Black Friday. It offers a higher resolution of 12.5MP native and 50MP mosaic, has more internal storage (225GB vs 115GB), and comes with a carbon fiber tripod (as opposed to aluminum) and a hard case, which are perhaps more suited for traveling to dark skies. We've been testing it out over the past few weeks and are incredibly impressed. The images we've taken of the moon, for example, are breathtaking. The Vespera Pro 2 is currently the highest resolution smart telescope on the market. View Deal Binoculars Big astronomy binoculars are more portable than a telescope, making them ideal for camping trips and spontaneous stargazing outings. (Image credit: Jase Parnell-Brookes) If you're looking for a pair of binoculars you can take anywhere, with excellent optical quality and edge-to-edge sharpness, the Celestron Regal ED 10x42 is an excellent investment. The ED glass eliminates chromatic aberration, and it has field-flattening lenses to correct curvature, resulting in sharp, bright and detailed images with basically no defects. Perfect for observing the moon and stars with excellent clarity. We have seen them cheaper at the start of the year, but over the summer they've been $379, so this price is worth taking advantage of. Read our full Celestron Regal ED 10x42 review If birdwatching is more your thing, the 8x42 variant is also in the Black Friday sale . View Deal Celestron Nature DX ED 8x42: was $229.95 now $189.04 If the Regal ED is a little out of budget, the Nature DX ED range is an excellent, more affordable alternative that still offers great image quality. This variant in particular is ideal for birdwatching, thanks to the 8x magnification, and the ED glass is ideal for following birds in flight. Plus, you can enjoy views of the moon and get a closer look at the stars. We have reviewed the Celestron Nature DX ED 10x42 variant, although this model isn't included in the Black Friday deals. View Deal Big astronomy binoculars are a must for any sky-lover, and the Celestron SkyMaster Pro ED 15x70 are perfect for getting detailed views of the moon, stars and even spotting Jupiter's moons. They typically fluctuate between $279 and $309, and although they aren't currently listed as a Black Friday offer, the $25 you can apply at checkout makes them the same price as the variant without ED glass . Personally, we'd always buy the pair with ED glass. Read our full Celestron SkyMaster Pro ED 15x70 review View Deal With a massive 20x magnification and 80mm objective lenses, these are serious skywatching binoculars that provide stunning detail in the night sky. They're perfect for close-up views of the moon and stars, and you can also spot Jupiter's moons and some of the brighter deep-sky objects. This is the cheapest we've seen them since June, and they tend to fluctuate between around $270 and $319. Read our full Celestron SkyMaster Pro 20x80 review The Pro ED version is also discounted , although not labelled as a Black Friday deal. There's a $30 coupon you can apply at checkout to get them down to $319.97. View Deal Star projectors (Image credit: Tantse Walter) The Pococo Galaxy Projector is one of our favorites, striking a nice balance between good-quality projections, a variety of available discs and a reasonable price — and no awful green laser stars. It comes in a choice of three colors (white, black and a pink/blue ombre), all of which are now at the same low price. The price tends to fluctuate throughout the year, usually between $79 and $99, but this is the cheapest we've seen it. It comes with the 'Westerlund2' galaxy disc and 'Diamond Stars' disc, and you can buy additional discs via their website. Read our full Pococo Galaxy Projector review View Deal 13-in-1 star projector: was $34.99 now $28.48 If what you're looking for is more in the realm of "a pretty light", then this star projector is a good one to go for. That said, it's still a pretty decent projector! It comes with 13 different discs, including the solar system, Earth, Moon, a black hole and various nebulas and galaxies. Not sure how relaxed we'd feel staring at a black hole in our bedroom without having some sort of existential crisis, but there are plenty of others to enjoy instead. We've tried similar models, which we've enjoyed, and the reviews look really positive. Plus, no awful green laser stars. View Deal One for the kids, here. This astronaut star projector doesn't produce realistic projections of the night sky, but it's a great way to get your kids to sleep and there's still a good amount of customization. There are 8 different nebula effects to choose from, and you can adjust the brightness, rotation speed and breathing rate (this mimics the twinkling effect). It does have the dreaded green laser stars, but at this price, and considering it's for kids — we'll allow it. Also...it's really cute. We've reviewed a similar model here. View Deal Dark Skys DS-FX projector: was £126.42 now £90.3 In a similar fashion to the Pococo projector, this one works with slides to project realistic imagery into your home. It comes with a Northern Hemisphere Chrome Star disc and has just three buttons on the unit itself to control it — no messing around with a remote control or app. We noticed that the motor is almost completely silent, making it an excellent sleep aid, and it's rechargeable, so you aren't limited to keeping it near an outlet. title: 'You had one job': Astrophysicist and Star Trek science advisor Erin MacDonald on the secret to her success and the science flubs that haunt her
summary: Live Science spoke with astrophysicist Erin Macdonald about her role as a science adviser for 'Star Trek' and other Hollywood movies.
content: From gravitational waves to time travel , science has always been at the heart of "Star Trek". While the franchise has never shied away from imagining the impossible, much of its appeal comes from making strange situations seem believable. That's where the role of a science adviser comes in. It's not necessarily about making sure everything is scientifically accurate, but understanding the science well enough to know where creative liberties can be taken and how to make them come alive on screen. Erin Macdonald knows this balance all-too-well. After studying general relativity and gravitational waves for her doctorate and spending years working at Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory (LIGO), Macdonald shifted gears and became a science advisor for six "Star Trek" series, including the "Discovery" franchise, as well as a variety of other television and film projects. Live Science spoke with Macdonald about how she brings the world of "Star Trek" to life, and her job's biggest pitfalls. KHC: How did you end up getting into the field of science advising? EM: After I got my Ph.D. and did a little bit of research, I realized academia and that world just weren't really for me. So I went into engineering, but I really missed teaching and being able to engage with students. I was trying to find more opportunities to do public science communication. I'm a big sci-fi nerd, so I started going to sci-fi conventions and giving solo panels and workshops that were basically, "Here's the physics behind faster-than-light travel ," and "Here's all the physics in 'Star Trek'." SCIENCE BEHIND THE CAMERA This article is part of a series called " Science Behind the Camera " which focuses on the role of science advisors. From helping to create engaging stories to set design and script rewrites, these experts shape some of the most compelling narratives on screen. Through that particular talk and just life happening, I met a lot of people on the convention circuit. I decided I wanted to go to L.A. I learned that science advising was a job, so I moved out there, still working as an engineer. CBS and "Star Trek" got wind of my talks, and they invited me to give presentations at their official licensed "Star Trek" events. That's how I got on their radar. A couple of years later, we were in a world where there were a lot of 'Star Trek' shows being produced, and they were looking for a science adviser for " Star Trek: Discovery ". [Editor's Note: "Star Trek: Discovery" ran for five seasons (65 episodes) from Sept. 2017, to May 2024 on CBS] That went well, and they brought me on as an in-house science adviser. KHC: You've now advised on how many shows? EM: Well, six "Star Trek" shows, but I'm starting to lose track of the films and other shows I've been called into for either one-off things or bigger jobs. It's been a great experience. I think a lot of being successful in L.A. and Hollywood is that every job is an audition for your next job. You work on one show, everyone goes their separate ways and works on new shows, and if they know someone they might want to bring in, they'll give you a call. I've been very lucky in that regard. KHC: What does the day-to-day look like for a science adviser? EM: All the jobs I've done are different. When I get pulled in to talk to someone about a new project, it could be almost anything. The biggest role, and the one I enjoy the most, is being brought in when a show is just getting off the ground and the writers' room is being established. They'll bring me in to sit in that writers' room and help contribute to the ideas and stories as they're being developed. If questions come up in real time, I can help answer them. That's the most ideal scenario for being a science adviser because you can get ahead of any issues as plots are starting to be developed. A lot of the time, when you're doing something wild like that, I'll just say, "Great, don't explain it. Do your thing. Try not to science it." Erin Macdonald But it can also look like being handed production scripts. Basically, they've gone through the whole process, they're nearing the point where they're going to start filming, and they're like, "Hey, can you check this for us?" That can be a blessing and a curse because it's a little less work, but then you can't course-correct as much if there are big plot problems. You have to find a way to work with the story and try to get the science as accurate as possible. In that scenario, it can end up being, "Don't explain it. Take these lines out. You're getting yourself in trouble. Leave everything else." The last kind of job, and one I've had a lot of colleagues do, is set design. They'll be brought in when they're building sets or doing post-production and want to make sure what's on screen looks science-y. The best example I can give is someone writing all the equations on "The Big Bang Theory". All those whiteboards you see? That's a scientist coming in to write all of that. Science advisors may help with set design, such as writing the equations on the whiteboards in CBS's popular show "The Big Bang Theory." (Image credit: CBS Photo Archive / Getty Images) I worked on a show called " Good American Family " on Hulu. It's not a science show at all, but they had a kid who was really interested in physics. I went in and wrote all the equations and talked to the actor about how to say the things he was going to be saying. The process can vary greatly. Even within "Star Trek", my relationship has been different from show to show. That's an exciting part of it, but I think people can see that it's a very varied position. KHC: Out of all your 7 years of experience in science advising, is there a particular scene, moment, or script you're especially proud of? EM: There are certainly ones that are really close to my heart. I'll give a couple of examples. One was the season two finale of " Star Trek: Lower Decks ." I wasn't brought in until season two, At the end, the showrunner was basically like, "Hey, I have this vision, but we need to build the 'Star Trek' science around it." He just had a scene in his mind and wanted to build the story. We came up with this great story about an asteroid belt with a lot of charged particles that disrupted the [protective] shields. There was a lot of good technobabble in there, too. It was really fun. Watching that episode, it just feels like a really authentic "Star Trek" episode because of all the science in it. I'm really proud that I was able to contribute to that. If you spend your time just criticizing the science in films and TV, this is not the job for you. Erin Macdonald Another one that stands out to me is the musical episode of " Star Trek: Strange New Worlds ". That was one of the first times the show was taking one of these big swings. The show is kind of known for doing all these big swings now, but that was one of the first. A lot of the time, when you're doing something wild like that, I'll just say, "Great, don't explain it. Do your thing. Try not to science it." But they pushed back on me and said, "No, no, no. We need a science explanation." We really worked together and came up with a detailed science explanation. What I'm really proud of is that they created that ready room scene [Editor's note: a ready room scene is a dramatic sequence set usually in a command office before a major battle or mission] where Spock explains everything that's happening. It's probably one of the longest ready room scenes we've had in "Star Trek". It's like, "And then this, and then this, and this is why, and this is why, and this is why, and this is what we need to do." It's goofy, but there was a lot of science put into that episode, which was a really fun process. KHC: I would be remiss if I didn't bring up the creation of Dr. Erin. How did that character come about, and how have you felt about the impact of the character? EM: It's really funny. The character of Dr. Erin has now shown up in multiple series, video games, and comic books, which delights me. Macdonald's influence as a science adviser resulted in the creation of the character Dr. Erin, based on Macdonald herself. (Image credit: Netflix/Paramount & Erin Macdonald) The origin of it started on " Star Trek: Prodigy ". It was a "Star Trek" show aimed at children. They wanted me to come in not just to help make sure the science was right, but also to do more traditional science communication and help create a character who was a kid who wanted to be a scientist and talk about what that process is like. That's the character of Rok-Tahk, and she's adorable. As they were reaching the end of season one, the kids were going to Starfleet Academy, and the showrunners were like, "She has to meet Dr. Erin. She is who she is because of Erin." That was just one of the greatest honors. It was a quick, one-line mention, not even named in the episode. KHC: Is there anything you wish you could change from your perspective? EM : Yeah, there are a few that haunt me a little bit. There are some shows where I was really involved, we meshed well together, and I helped with the story. There are very few things I would change. But then there are other shows where I'm just given the script at the 11th hour. Plot-wise, would I have suggested something different? Yes. But it was too late to course-correct. One really good example was in "Star Trek: Discovery". They had an episode where they were trying to ride gravitational waves out of a nebula, as one does. They had that ready room explainer moment, and they were showing the gravitational waves as literal sine waves, like the ocean waves you think of. I was working with the visual effects team, and I pushed back. I said, "Really, these are compression waves." You could still make an argument that they were going to ride them out, but it's more like how sound waves move. They're compression waves. To their credit, they animated that and put it in the scene. But as people were watching it, they felt that the way we were talking about it versus what we were seeing just wasn't working. It was pulling people out of the scene, so they had to revert back. It was funny because when that aired, I had three or four former gravitational wave colleagues who were like, "Erin, you had one job." Gravitational waves are compression waves, like sound waves, as opposed to sine waves. (Image credit: MARK GARLICK/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY via Getty Images) Another quick example was an episode in season one of "Strange New Worlds" where Spock says, "We're being pulled into the black hole ." That's one of those moments where it's technically not correct. You fall into black holes. It's a very public misconception that I try to fight back against a lot. Black holes aren't hoovering things up. It's just deep gravity. But in the context of the scene, Spock is being very condescending and talking down to La'an, so he's simplifying the language for the public. I can sort of get away with that. KHC: Is there anything else you think our readers should know about science advising? EM: I meet a lot of people who, delicately or not, say, "I could do your job. I'd be a great science adviser." I think what's made me successful in science advising is that I take a very "yes, and" attitude. I'm a fan first and foremost. If you spend your time just criticizing the science in films and TV, this is not the job for you. You need to work with the stories you're given, and you need to understand the mission. Scientists say the story's not over yet. 'We only expect to encounter that once every 130 years': A huge new crater on the moon could mean a giant leap for lunar science There's a quick anecdote. I worked on another film called " Space Cadet ," which is a stoner comedy on Amazon, and they were having a really hard time finding a science adviser because everyone was trashing the script. It's ridiculous, goofy, and fun. They were like, "Look, we just want someone who makes sure the NASA people know what NASA people would say. That's it." And I was like, "Great, let's do it." The job isn't for everyone. Storytelling comes first. Editor's note: This interview has been edited and shortened for length and clarity.
